title: The great joinings: learning to see the world in the joining of two sounds
theme: The point where two sounds meet in recitation becomes a pattern for meditation: two terms, the junction between them and what joins them, found in the worlds, the lights, learning, family and the speaking body.

sandhi.rule: After ā a visarga is lost before a vowel, and the hiatus stays: saṃhitāyāḥ + upaniṣadam → saṃhitāyā upaniṣadam.
u before a dissimilar vowel becomes v: P. 6.1.77 (इको यणचि).
A final m before a vowel is simply joined to it; the five headings are written as one string.
A visarga after a vowel other than a or ā becomes r before a vowel: dyauḥ + uttararūpam → dyaur uttararūpam.

samasa.meaning: the lustre that comes from sacred knowledge
concerning the self, here the body

morphology.note: The enclitic dual of the first-person pronoun, ‘of us two’: the wish is made for a pair, student and teacher.

The five headings are avyayībhāva compounds of adhi with a noun, ‘in respect of …’. Kūranārāyaṇa and Rāmānanda name the rule, P. 2.1.6 (अव्ययं विभक्तिसमीपसमृद्धिव्यृद्ध्यर्थाभावात्ययासम्प्रतिशब्दप्रादुर्भावपश्चाद्यथाऽऽनुपूर्व्ययौगपद्यसादृश्यसम्पत्तिसाकल्यान्तवचनेषु), the indeclinable used ‘in the sense of a case ending’. Rāmānanda adds that adhyātmam takes the suffix ṭac by P. 5.4.108 (अनश्च).
Present middle of cakṣ with ā, ‘they call’. The subject is unexpressed: ‘people, those who know’.
Nominative singular of div / dyo, ‘sky’, feminine here.

translation.literal: Together [be] renown for us two; together for us two [be] the lustre of sacred knowledge. Now, therefore, we shall explain the secret teaching of the joining, in five domains: with regard to the worlds, with regard to the lights, with regard to learning, with regard to offspring, with regard to the person. These they call the great joinings. Now, with regard to the worlds: the earth [is] the prior form; the sky the latter form; space the junction;
translation.readable: May renown come to both of us together; may the lustre of sacred learning come to both of us together. Now, then, we will explain the hidden teaching of the joining, in five areas: the worlds, the lights, learning, offspring and the person. These are called the great joinings. First, the worlds: the earth is the first sound, the sky the second, the space between them the junction,

samasa.meaning: food that is to be eaten

morphology.note: hanu, ‘jaw’, is feminine here, as adharā and uttarā show.
Perfect of vid with present meaning, ‘knows’. Śaṅkara argues that here it means upāsanā, meditation: «वेदेत्युपासनं स्यात्».
Passive of dhā with sam, the very verb of the five joinings (sandhi, sandhāna): one who meditates on the joinings ‘is joined’ with their fruits.
suvarga is the Taittirīya form of svarga, ‘heaven’. The Sāyaṇa-pāṭha and Madhva’s text read suvargyeṇa, ‘leading to heaven’ (corrections.json).

translation.literal: Now with regard to the person: the lower jaw [is] the prior form; the upper jaw the latter form; speech the junction; the tongue the connector. Thus with regard to the person. These [are] the great joinings. Whoever thus knows these great joinings [as] explained is joined with offspring, with cattle, with the lustre of sacred knowledge, with food to eat, with the heavenly world.
translation.readable: Last, the person: the lower jaw is the first sound, the upper jaw the second, speech the junction, the tongue what joins them. These are the great joinings. Whoever meditates on them as they have been explained is joined with children and cattle, with the radiance of learning, with food, and with the heavenly world.

syntax: The anuvāka opens with a two-line wish without a verb (‘together for us two [be] renown … lustre’). Then a programmatic sentence with the future vyākhyāsyāmaḥ names the topic and lists five domains as indeclinable headings. Each domain is then set out in the same frame: ‘atha’ + heading; four nominal sentences of the form ‘X [is] the prior form / the latter form / the junction / the connector’; ‘iti’ + heading. The close is a relative sentence of fruit, ‘whoever knows (veda) … is joined (sandhīyate) with …’, with five instrumentals.

ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara: the student, because only the student still has something to gain — «शिष्यस्य हि अकृतार्थत्वात्प्रार्थनोपपद्यते». Kūranārāyaṇa: the teacher, who, about to give the knowledge, wishes its fruit to belong to both — «अथ शिष्याय विद्यां प्रदित्सुराचार्यो विद्याफलं शिष्यस्य स्वस्य च साधारणं भवत्वित्याशास्ते». The dual nau allows either.

Not the collection of Vedic hymns but the joining of sounds in continuous recitation (P. 1.4.109 (परः संनिकर्षः संहिता), which Gopālānanda cites). Rāmānanda’s example is the joining a + u = o: the a is the prior form, the u the latter, the o the junction, and the effort that produces it the connector. The ‘great saṃhitās’ apply this fourfold pattern to larger things.

veda ordinarily means ‘knows’. Śaṅkara argues that here it must mean meditation (upāsanā), since the context is one of practice and a parallel passage says ‘meditate’ («वेदेत्युपासनं स्यात्»). Kūranārāyaṇa agrees that the explanation is for the sake of meditation.

The base text and Śaṅkara’s mūla read suvargeṇa lokena, ‘with the heavenly world’; the Sāyaṇa-pāṭha and Madhva’s text read suvargyeṇa, ‘[with the world] leading to heaven’ (corrections.json, class variant). The sense differs little.

metre.name: prose
metre.note: Prose (brāhmaṇa style) throughout, in short nominal clauses; the four units are the recitation’s divisions, not stanzas.

beginner: When we speak quickly, words run together: two sounds meet and make a third. Teachers of recitation call that meeting a joining. This passage turns the joining into a way of looking at the world. Every joining has four parts: a first sound, a second sound, the place where they meet, and what brings them together. Now look at the earth and the sky: between them is space, and the wind connects them. Look at a teacher and a student: between them is learning, and teaching connects them. Look at a mother and a father: between them is a child, joined through birth. Even in your own mouth, the lower and upper jaw meet in speech, moved by the tongue. Practising this way of seeing, the passage promises, brings family, plenty and a good life.
analogy: Like a bridge: two banks, the river between them, and the span that joins them. Once you see that shape you start to see it everywhere — between people, between ideas, between generations.

commentary.q: What does the passage actually say?
commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: After a wish that renown and the lustre of sacred knowledge come to ‘us two’ together, it announces the ‘upaniṣad of the saṃhitā’ in five domains and sets out each in four terms: in the worlds, earth, sky, space, wind; in the lights, fire, sun, waters, lightning; in learning, teacher, pupil, knowledge, teaching; in offspring, mother, father, child, procreation; in the person, lower jaw, upper jaw, speech, tongue. It calls these the great saṃhitās and promises that whoever ‘knows’ them is joined with offspring, cattle, lustre, food and the heavenly world. It does not say what one is to do with the correspondences; that is the commentators’ question.

commentary.q: Why do student and teacher pray for renown together?
commentary.label: comparative
commentary.text: Śaṅkara takes the wish as the student’s: the teacher has already reached his goal, so a prayer from him would make no sense («कृतार्थो ह्याचार्यो नाम भवति»). Kūranārāyaṇa makes it the teacher’s, with an image: when a daughter is given in marriage, the children belong to the bridegroom’s family alone — «यथा कस्मैचिद्वराय प्रतिपादितायां कन्यायां पुत्रादिकं फलं तस्यैव वरस्य भवति» — and the teacher asks that it not be so with knowledge. Rāmānanda distinguishes this prayer from the opening ‘śaṃ no mitraḥ’: that belonged to the whole Upaniṣad, this one to the meditation on the saṃhitā («सम्प्रति संहितोपनिषदङ्गभूता प्रार्थना क्रियते»).

commentary.q: Why begin with meditations on sound rather than on Brahman?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara: a mind long shaped by memorising the text cannot be brought all at once to the knowledge of meaning, so the Upaniṣad first gives a way of seeing that stays close to the text — «यतोऽत्यर्थं ग्रन्थभाविता बुद्धिर्न शक्यते सहसार्थज्ञानविषयेऽवतारयितुमित्यतः». Rāmānanda gives the same reason in his own words: the mind first takes hold of the form of the words and only then passes to their meaning («शब्दस्वरूपे सङ्क्रान्ता बुद्धिरर्थस्वरूपे क्रमेणैव सङ्क्रामति»). The anuvāka is a bridge from recitation to reflection.

commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: Śaṅkara: on the prior sound of a joining one is to place the view ‘earth’ — «संहितायाः पूर्वे वर्णे पृथिवीदृष्टिः कर्तव्येत्युक्तं भवति» — and so on for each term. Rāmānanda makes the pattern concrete with the sandhi a + u → o: «तत्राकारः पूर्वरूपम्», the u the latter form, the o the junction «ओकारः सन्धिर्द्वयोर्वर्णयोः सन्निकर्षरूपत्वादोकारस्य», and the effort that produces it the connector. Kūranārāyaṇa identifies that effort with breath: the wind is ‘the effort for pronouncing the prior and latter together’ («पूर्वोत्तरयोः सहोच्चारणार्थो यो यत्नः स वायुरिति वेदितव्यः»). Rāmānanda adds that the saṃhitā meant is that of one’s own branch of the Veda («सेयं संहिता स्वशाखासम्बद्धैव ग्राह्या»).

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara uses the word veda in the last sentence to define meditation exactly: a continuous flow of the same idea, as scripture prescribes, unmixed with other ideas, resting on a support the scripture gives — «उपासनं च यथाशास्त्रं तुल्यप्रत्ययसन्ततिरसङ्कीर्णा च अतत्प्रत्ययैः शास्त्रोक्तालम्बनविषया च». He compares the everyday sense: one ‘attends on’ a teacher or a king by serving them continually, and gains the fruit of that service.

commentary.q: Is the promised fruit the point?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The text promises offspring, cattle, lustre, food and heaven, and Śaṅkara simply restates it: «प्रजादिफलं प्राप्नोतीत्यर्थः». Rāmānanda distinguishes two practitioners: one who meditates without desire attains the knowledge of Brahman, one who meditates with desire gets the stated fruit — «एतासां पञ्चानां संहितोपनिषदामनुष्ठानेन निष्कामस्य उपासितुः ब्रह्मविद्यानिष्पत्तिः भवति». Kūranārāyaṇa reasons that since knowing the joinings has no visible result of its own, the explanation is meant for meditation («अत्र संहिताज्ञाने दृष्टान्यफलादर्शनात् संहिताव्याख्यानमिदम् उपासनार्थम्»).

advaita.text: For Śaṅkara the anuvāka belongs to the region of meditation and its fruits, not of liberating knowledge. It is a graded step: the mind trained on the text is led to a way of seeing ‘close to the text’ («ग्रन्थसन्निकृष्टामेव व्याख्यास्यामः»), and the word ‘knows’ is read as meditation. Its fruits — offspring to heaven — are stated without reinterpretation.

visistadvaita.text: Kūranārāyaṇa reads the opening wish as the teacher’s and the five joinings as meditations. Rāmānanda reads the fruit two ways: for one who meditates without desire it is the knowledge of Brahman («निष्कामस्य उपासितुः ब्रह्मविद्यानिष्पत्तिः भवति»), for one with desire the fruit the text names. Kūranārāyaṇa’s opening verse (printed before 1.1) says that in the Sāṃhitī too the Lord of all is taught as ‘the one who joins’: «सांहितीष्वपि सन्धाता सर्वेशः प्रतिपाद्यते». The word sandhātā echoes this anuvāka’s sandhāna; it suggests that for him the connector of every joining is finally the Lord. That is an inference from the verse — his comment on this anuvāka does not say it.

dvaita.text: Madhva’s comment on this anuvāka is a single line: in the five, the worlds and the rest, are the forms of Nārāyaṇa and others — «नारायणादिरूपाणि लोकादिषु च पञ्चसु». For him the terms of each joining are to be meditated on as forms of the Lord present in them. The line is too short to say how each correspondence is read.

schools.disagreement: All agree that the anuvāka teaches meditations on the joining of sounds and that its fruits are worldly as stated. They differ on who speaks the opening wish (the student for Śaṅkara, the teacher for Kūranārāyaṇa), and on what the terms of the joinings ultimately are: mental supports placed on the sounds (Śaṅkara), meditations that can ripen into knowledge of Brahman when done without desire (Rāmānanda), or forms of Nārāyaṇa (Madhva).

parallels.note: Four anuvākas later the Śīkṣāvallī sets out another system of correspondences, groups of five in the outer world and in the person, and concludes that ‘all this is fivefold’. The great joinings are its first exercise in seeing one pattern in many domains.

contemporary.text: The passage places the teacher and the pupil on the same footing as earth and sky: two terms that only make sense with the space between them and the act that connects them. Leaders often think of themselves as the first term and others as the second. The passage asks about the junction and the connector — what actually passes between people, and what makes it pass. In a team, that is shared knowledge and the work of explaining. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: Pick two people you know well. What is the ‘space between’ you, and what keeps you connected?
reflect.deeper: Why might a text use the joining of two sounds as a pattern for the worlds, learning and family? What does that say about how it regards speech?
reflect.practice: Say a phrase slowly where two words run together. Notice the first sound, the second, where they meet, and the movement of the tongue that joins them.

references.text: Kūranārāyaṇa and Rāmānanda name the grammatical rules for the five headings (avyayībhāva compounds, P. 2.1.6 (अव्ययं विभक्तिसमीपसमृद्धिव्यृद्ध्यर्थाभावात्ययासम्प्रतिशब्दप्रादुर्भावपश्चाद्यथाऽऽनुपूर्व्ययौगपद्यसादृश्यसम्पत्तिसाकल्यान्तवचनेषु); the samāsānta ṭac, P. 5.4.108 (अनश्च)) and for mahāsaṃhitā (P. 2.1.61 (सन्महत्परमोत्तमोत्कृष्टाः पूज्यमानैः)); these are their analyses.
Gopālānanda (modern) calls this the first step of a graded path: meditation on sound first, then on meaning.

flags.note: suvargeṇa (base, Śaṅkara) against suvargyeṇa (Sāyaṇa-pāṭha, Madhva’s text); four spacing corrections and one keying correction (अथाधिलोकम्) to the base (corrections.json).
Whether the opening wish is the student’s or the teacher’s is disputed among the commentators; the text does not say.
